title: From structural changes to diffraction and  phonon  data
summary: Connect structural phase transitions, orientation domains and real calculation results through order parameters, scattering phases and mass-weighted displacements.
scope: The Landau calculation uses the dimensionless single-component model F=aQ²+bQ⁴+cQ⁶−hQ. Its parameters do not represent measured BaTiO₃ temperatures, polarization, or free energies.

The BaTiO₃ example fixes an ideal cubic parent cell and moves only Ti to illustrate six  polarity  directional domains. It is not a full phase diagram, actual  soft mode  eigenvector,  domain wall  structure, or phase-transition-path calculation.

Diffraction uses the specified structure and constant real scattering weights to calculate a kinematic structure factor. |F|² is a model intensity; it omits realistic angle-dependent atomic form factors, thermal motion, absorption, instrument effects and multiple-scattering corrections.

The Phonopy module reads previously calculated compatible data such as band.yaml or qpoints.yaml. It neither runs first-principles calculations nor reconstructs force constants, IR/Raman activity, or actual spectral intensities from frequency files. Built-in data are synthetic teaching samples.

sources.title: ISODISTORT official help: distortion modes, subgroups, and equivalent domains
sources.note: Use this to check the concepts of parent groups, distortion stabilizers and equivalent domains. This site implements an explicitly specified polar teaching model and does not provide the software’s complete subgroup search.

sources.title: IUCr Online Dictionary of Crystallography: Structure factor
sources.note: phase convention  of structure factors and the kinematic-scattering background. Integer weights, hand calculations, and exercises in this lesson are original.

sources.title: IUCr Online Dictionary of Crystallography: Reflection conditions
sources.note: Reflection conditions from centering, screws, and glides, distinguishing general space-group conditions from additional special-occupation conditions. This site derives the specific conditions independently from phases.

sources.title: Phonopy official documentation: Output files
sources.note: Check fields including band.yaml, qpoints.yaml, q-position, frequency, eigenvector, the number of primitive-cell atoms and path distances.

sources.title: Official Phonopy documentation: Formulations
sources.note: Verify  mass weighting   dynamical matrix , complex eigenvectors, atomic-displacement  phase convention , and frequency units.

lessons.title: How does the free-energy curve determine equilibrium?
lessons.summary: Find stationary points, check curvature, then compare free energies; distinguish local stability from global equilibrium.

sections.title: State the model and normalization first
sections.text: Here Q is a dimensionless distortion amplitude along a specified polar direction and h its conjugate bias. Coefficients multiply powers of Q directly, without additional 1/2, 1/4, or 1/6 prefactors. With zero bias and an inversion-symmetric parent phase, Q and −Q are equivalent, so the free energy contains only even powers.

sections.title: Stationarity only establishes zero slope
sections.text: Differentiate once with respect to Q and set the derivative to zero. For the quartic model with h=0, c=0 and b>0, Q=0 is always stationary; when a<0, there are also two nonzero stationary points. List all roots before assessing stability: not every root of the stationarity equation is an equilibrium phase.
sections.formula: F′=2aQ+4bQ³+6cQ⁵−h; for c=h=0, Q=0 or Q²=−a/(2b)

sections.title: Curvature determines local behavior
sections.text: At a stationary point, F″>0 indicates a local minimum and F″<0 a local maximum. If F″=0, the second-derivative test is inconclusive, so inspect higher-order terms; for example, with a=0, b>0 and c=h=0, Q=0 remains a quartic flat-bottomed minimum.

sections.title: Global equilibrium requires comparing energies
sections.text: For a free energy bounded below, compare F at all local minima; the lowest is the global equilibrium. A sixth-order model with b<0、c>0 may have both central and nonzero local minima, so positive curvature alone cannot identify the favored phase. Positive h favors positive Q, but this does not calculate actual domain-switching rates or hysteresis dynamics.

examples.title: Work out a symmetric double well by hand
steps: Set a=−1, b=1, c=h=0 to obtain F=−Q²+Q⁴.
F′=−2Q+4Q³=0 gives Q=0 and ±1/√2.
F″(0)=−2, so the center is a maximum; F″(±1/√2)=4, so the two side points are minima.
F(0)=0 and F(±1/√2)=−1/4; the two sides are degenerate global minima.
examples.result: Positive and negative amplitudes are equivalent. This is a double well along a one-dimensional directional slice, not the full three-dimensional six-domain energy surface.

lessons.title: From the parent group to six polar orientation domains
lessons.summary: Use stabilizers and group orbits to understand six equivalent directions, distinguishing a single domain's symmetry from that of the entire domain set.

sections.title: The operations retained by a distortion form a subgroup
sections.text: Let the parent point group be G and choose order-parameter vector Q. Only operations preserving Q itself belong to that domain's stabilizer H. Operations mapping Q to another equivalent direction belong to the parent group but are no longer symmetries of this single domain.

sections.title: Fix a structural model that can be checked
sections.text: Use an ideal ABO₃ parent cell: Ba at (0,0,0), Ti at (1/2,1/2,1/2), and three O atoms at (1/2,1/2,0), (1/2,0,1/2), (0,1/2,1/2). Displace only Ti slightly along +z, leaving other positions and the cubic lattice fixed. The point group falls from m−3m to 4mm, which preserves a +z polar vector; this coordinate model has space group P4mm. An accidentally cubic lattice metric does not imply cubic symmetry of the full structure.

sections.title: Six directions follow from the group index
sections.text: The parent point group Oh has 48 operations, and the C4v stabilizer of the +z domain has 8, giving a six-element orbit: ±x, ±y and ±z. The translation subgroup is unchanged here, so these are six orientation domains, with no additional antiphase domains. +z and −z differ by 180°, while +z and +x differ by 90°.

sections.title: Domain directions are not a domain-wall model
sections.text: Interactive switching displays each uniform domain and its retained operations, without calculating how domains join.  domain wall  width, energy, bound charge, and switching dynamics additionally require gradients, elasticity, and electrostatics. Moving Ti alone is also not the actual  soft mode  of BaTiO₃: real modes generally involve coordinated responses of multiple atoms and strain.

examples.title: Why is inversion not a symmetry of a single +z domain?
steps: The polar vector Q=(0,0,Q0) becomes (0,0,−Q0) under inversion.
For Q0≠0, the new vector differs from the original, so inversion does not belong to the +z domain's  stabilizer .
The parent phase contains inversion, so it maps the +z domain to the equivalent −z domain.
examples.result: An operation can connect two domains without belonging to the symmetry retained by either domain.

lessons.title: Turn mass-weighted eigenvectors into atomic motion
lessons.summary: Distinguish eigenvector components, physical displacements, and arbitrary animation amplitudes to establish coordinate conventions for soft-mode freezing and data import.

sections.title: Force constants differ from  dynamical matrix
sections.text: Force constants are second derivatives of potential energy with respect to atomic displacements; the dynamical matrix also includes mass factors. In matrix notation at Γ, D=M^(−1/2)ΦM^(−1/2). Its eigenvalues correspond to squared angular frequencies, so its eigenvectors cannot be treated directly as physical displacements with the same scaling for all atoms.

sections.title: Divide each atom's components by the square root of its own mass
sections.text: For a real Γ-point mode, a single-mode displacement can be written uj=Qej/√mj; Q's physical dimensions depend on normalization. Equal e components for unequal-mass atoms do not imply equal physical displacements. The lesson animation has an additional global magnification that changes only display scale, not thermal or zero-point amplitudes.

sections.title: Rigid-translation eigenvectors need not have equal lengths
sections.text: For two atoms of masses 1 and 4 undergoing equal parallel displacements, the normalized  mass weighting  vector can be (1,2)/√5. Dividing by √m gives displacement 1/√5 for both. Conversely, (2,−1)/√5 corresponds to displacements (2,−1/2)/√5, whose  mass weighting  total displacement vanishes and can represent relative motion in this one-dimensional two-mass model.

sections.title: Finite q also requires complex phases
sections.text: Phonopy outputs complex Cartesian eigenvectors. Under its phase convention, reconstructing finite-q displacements requires the Bloch phase from equilibrium atomic positions and lattice translations. Here q and x use matching reduced coordinates and ℓ is an integer cell coordinate. Degenerate subspaces permit basis changes and the overall complex phase is arbitrary; different arrow directions alone do not establish a physical contradiction between two files.

examples.title: Equal e components are not equal displacements
steps: Suppose two atoms have equal nonzero e components and masses of 1 and 4.
The displacement ratio is (e/√1)/(e/√4)=2.
For a rigid translation, use e2/e1=√(4/1)=2 instead.
examples.result: To identify a rigid translation, check the physical displacements rather than comparing raw eigenvector numbers alone.

lessons.title: A diffraction peak is a vector sum of atomic scattering phases
lessons.summary: Add scattering arrows one by one in the complex plane to understand amplitude, intensity, and coordinate-origin dependence.

sections.title: Positions set phases; weights set arrow lengths
sections.text: Sum complex amplitudes using  conventional cell   fractional coordinates  xj, integer reflection indices hkl, and real constant weights fj. Constant weights make hand calculation convenient; actual X-ray scattering factors usually vary with scattering vector and may include complex corrections.

sections.title: Sum amplitudes first, then take the squared modulus
sections.text: Two equally weighted scatterers lie at (0,0,0) and (1/2,0,0). For odd h their arrows point oppositely and cancel; for even h they add in phase. Summing individual atomic intensities loses coherent interference and cannot reproduce this contrast.

sections.title: A rigid translation changes only the overall phase
sections.text: Translating every atom by δ multiplies F by a unit-modulus phase and leaves |F|² unchanged. Moving only one sublattice changes relative phases and generally changes intensity. This directly distinguishes an origin change from an actual structural distortion.

sections.title: Brightness is not a complete experimental spectrum
sections.text: This calculation gives structural amplitudes and relative model intensities. Powder peak profiles, geometric and polarization factors, thermal motion, absorption, preferred orientation and multiple scattering are not automatically supplied by this single sum. A weak reflection in the current model cannot immediately be called a symmetry-enforced systematic absence.

examples.title: Destructive and constructive addition of two unit arrows
steps: Choose (0,0,0) and (1/2,0,0), each with f=1.
The phases for 100 are 0 and π, so F100=1−1=0.
The phases for 200 are 0 and 2π, so F200=2 and I200=4.
examples.result: Scattering phases explain extinction; the incoherent sum of two atomic intensities, 2, cannot replace |F|².

lessons.title: Centering extinctions, basis extinctions and accidental cancellation
lessons.summary: Compare Si, GaAs, and NaCl to distinguish chemical occupations in the same F lattice and assign a precise cause to zero intensity.

sections.title: Factor out the common F-centering factor first
sections.text: Conventional face-centered cell translation representatives are (0,0,0), (0,1/2,1/2), (1/2,0,1/2), (1/2,1/2,0). Their phase sum is 4 only when h,k,l are all odd or all even, and vanishes for mixed parity. The I-lattice condition is h+k+l even.

sections.title: The Si diamond basis adds another condition
sections.text: The two identical scatterers in the Si basis are offset by (1/4,1/4,1/4). After applying the F-centering condition, multiply by 1+exp[iπ(h+k+l)/2]. Thus, although 200 has all-even indices, its basis factor vanishes; the basis factor for 220 is 2. The basis factor is nonzero for all-odd reflections.

sections.title: Identical geometric offsets do not guarantee identical extinctions
sections.text: GaAs occupies the two sites with different elements, changing the basis factor to fGa+fAs exp[iπ(h+k+l)/2]. Thus F200=4(fGa−fAs) is not universally forbidden by F centering. If equal user-specified weights happen to cancel, this is cancellation in that weight model, not a forbidden reflection of  zinc blende   space group  under every scattering condition.

sections.title: NaCl provides another chemical comparison
sections.text: Use two F sublattices, with Cl offset by (1/2,1/2,1/2) from Na. Allowed all-odd reflections give 4(fNa−fCl); all-even reflections give 4(fNa+fCl). Intensity comparisons must specify weights, cell choice, and normalization. Record general space-group conditions separately from additional special-occupation conditions.

examples.title: The 200 reflection in three materials
steps: The 200 reflections of all three structures satisfy the all-even F-centering condition.
Set the constant Si weight to 1: F200=4(1−1)=0.
examples.result: These numbers are hand-calculation models with specified weights. They compare interference mechanisms, not measured peak intensities of the three materials.

lessons.title: How do screw axes and glide planes restrict reflections?
lessons.summary: First check whether the rotational part preserves the reciprocal vector, then derive extinctions on specific reflection rows or planes from translation phases.

sections.title: Check both rotation and translation parts
sections.text: For a chemical-label-preserving operation {R|t}, the structure-factor constraint Fh=exp(2πi h·t)Fh applies only to reflections satisfying Rᵀh=h. If this phase is not 1, Fh must vanish. Ignoring Rᵀh=h incorrectly extends a condition for one reflection row to all hkl.

sections.title: 2₁  screw axis  along z
sections.text: The operation maps (x,y,z) to (−x,−y,z+1/2). Its rotation preserves 00l, and its translation phase is exp(iπl). Thus, 00l is not forbidden by this operation only when l is even. General hkl do not all satisfy the invariance condition, so this screw axis alone does not extinguish every odd-l reflection.

sections.title: c  glide plane  with normal along x
sections.text: Take (x,y,z)→(−x,y,z+1/2), with mirror normal along x and glide c/2. The mirror preserves the reflection plane 0kl, and the translation phase is again exp(iπl). Therefore l must be even within 0kl; for h≠0, this glide operation alone does not justify that criterion.

sections.title: An allowed condition does not guarantee a strong peak
sections.text: Satisfying a reflection condition means only that the operation does not force the amplitude to vanish. Other operations, basis occupancies or particular scattering weights may still cancel the sum. The interactive screw model checks phases; it is not an automatic extinction table covering all 230 space groups and settings.

examples.title: Why does the same half translation apply to different reflection sets?
steps: The rotation of 2₁(z) maps (h, k, l)→(−h,−k, l); invariance requires h=k=0.
The mirror part of a c-glide sends (h,k,l)→(−h,k,l), so invariance requires only h=0.
Both have t=(0,0,1/2), so both test (−1)^l, but one applies to a row and the other to a plane.
examples.result: The rotational part determines the invariant reflection set; the translation phase determines parity conditions.

lessons.title: Read Phonopy files as interpretable data
lessons.summary: Check primitive cells, branch counts, units, and path segments, preserving the physical information actually contained in frequency data.

sections.title: The two file types answer different questions
sections.text: band.yaml normally contains q points, distances, and frequencies calculated along a chosen path; qpoints.yaml gives selected q points that need not form a continuous path. phonopy.yaml mainly stores configuration and structure. Sharing a file extension does not guarantee a phonon list suitable for dispersion plotting.
sections.formula: phonon[i] → q-position, band[j] → frequency, eigenvector (if output)

sections.title: Check dimensions and fields first
sections.text: For N atoms per primitive cell, every complete q point should have 3N modes. Eigenvectors should be organized by N atoms, three Cartesian components each, and real and imaginary parts for each component. Frequencies without eigenvectors cannot reconstruct mode animations; without masses or structure, actual atomic displacements cannot be claimed.

sections.title: Retain path segments and units
sections.text: Break curves between discontinuous path segments rather than connecting endpoints by a line that implies calculated intermediate wave vectors. qpoints data can be displayed as sampled points, but this is not a continuous dispersion. Frequencies are often in THz, but other conversion settings are possible; confirm units when importing instead of inferring them from the filename. Path distances also depend on the input length convention.

sections.title: Importing results does not supply missing physical quantities
sections.text: A single high-symmetry path does not uniformly sample the entire  Brillouin zone . A histogram of path frequencies is therefore not a  phonon  density of states. Frequencies and eigenvectors alone also provide neither Raman tensors nor mode effective charges. The built-in sample is synthetic data designed to test paths, complex phases, and animation, not a first-principles prediction for Si, GaAs, or BaTiO₃.

examples.title: What can a frequency file establish?
steps: natom=2 and six frequency entries per q point: the branch count is consistent.
Without eigenvector, available frequencies and path information can still be displayed.
If eigenvectors, masses and atomic coordinates are complete, reconstruct relative motion using the stated convention.
Without effective charges or Raman derivatives, spectral activity and absolute intensities are not assigned automatically.
examples.result: The interface should accurately reflect the information supported by the input and retain missing-field notices.

lessons.title: Imaginary frequencies, soft modes and the next structural checks
lessons.summary: Translate displayed minus signs back into a negative-curvature question, then use numerical convergence and frozen displacements to distinguish physical clues from computational errors.

sections.title: A displayed negative sign usually encodes a negative eigenvalue
sections.text: Harmonic dynamical-matrix eigenvalues are ω². A negative value gives imaginary ω; plots often mark this with a negative real magnitude, not a negative frequency oscillating backward. Only a stable harmonic oscillator has real periodic time evolution. A back-and-forth animation of an imaginary-frequency mode illustrates its shape only.

sections.title: Softening reflects potential-energy curvature
sections.text: A decreasing mode frequency indicates a weaker harmonic restoring force in that direction. If the approximation and reference structure are converged, a negative eigenvalue suggests locally decreasing energy along that direction. It does not alone determine the final low-temperature phase, transition temperature, or unavoidable instability of a real sample; anharmonicity, stress conditions, and finite temperature affect the conclusion.

sections.title: First check numerical issues and the reference state
sections.text: Check whether the structure is sufficiently relaxed and residual forces and stress are acceptable; compare supercell sizes, electronic sampling, displacement amplitudes and force-constant accuracy. Very small negative acoustic frequencies near Γ particularly require checks of translational invariance and convergence. Finding no imaginary frequencies along one path does not establish stability throughout the Brillouin zone or at finite temperature.

sections.title: Then validate along the mode under controlled conditions
sections.text: With complete eigenvectors, masses, and phases, construct small-amplitude frozen structures for r(Q)=r0+Qe/√m and verify curvature using independent energy calculations. Finite q additionally requires compatible  supercell  and correct spatial phases. Fitting energy points to a Landau polynomial connects to the preceding lesson, but one harmonic frequency supplies neither all higher-order coefficients nor an experimental phase diagram automatically.

examples.title: After seeing a displayed value of −0.05 near Γ
steps: First check units and the plotting sign convention; do not read the number directly as a stable period.
Check whether this is an acoustic branch and inspect residual forces in the reference structure.
Increase numerical accuracy, check the acoustic translation condition and see whether the negative value persists.
If the evidence supports negative curvature, independently check energy along that mode.
examples.result: The number is a clue requiring interpretation. Here −0.05 is an illustrative value, not an actual result for any material.

exercises.title: From derivatives to the global minima of a double well
exercises.prompt: Take F(Q)=−Q²+Q⁴ with all quantities dimensionless. Differentiate, find roots, assess curvature, and compare energies in sequence.

steps.prompt: What is F′(Q)?
steps.hint: Differentiate the quadratic and quartic terms separately.
choices: −Q+Q³
−2Q+4Q³
steps.explanation: This model has no 1/2 or 1/4 prefactors, so its derivative is −2Q+4Q³.

steps.prompt: What are all the real stationary points?
steps.hint: Factor out 2Q, leaving −1+2Q².
choices: Only 0
steps.explanation: Q=0 or Q²=1/2 gives three real stationary points.

steps.prompt: What are the local properties of these three points?
choices: All three are minima
0 is a minimum; both side points are maxima
0 is a maximum; the two side points are minima
steps.explanation: The central curvature is −2 and the side curvatures are 4; their signs indicate opposite local behavior.

steps.prompt: What is the free energy at the two side minima?
steps.hint: Substitute Q²=1/2 and Q⁴=1/4 into F.
choices: −1/4, with both degenerate
−1/2, and only positive Q is stable
0, the same as the center
steps.explanation: F=−1/2+1/4=−1/4, below the central value 0. The positive quartic term bounds the model below, making the side minima global.

exercises.title: Count directional domains using  stabilizer
exercises.prompt: For the parent point group Oh, choose the nonzero polar vector Q=(0,0,Q0). Its C4v stabilizer has 8 elements; the parent group has 48, and the translation subgroup remains unchanged.

steps.prompt: Which condition defines this single domain's stabilizer?
steps.hint: The selected vector itself must be preserved.
choices: D(g)Q can be any vector of the same length
D(g)Q=Q
D(g)Q=−Q
steps.explanation: Mapping Q to another direction connects different domains; it is not a symmetry of this single domain.

steps.prompt: How many equivalent directional domains exist?
steps.hint: Use the orbit–stabilizer relation.
steps.explanation: 48/8=6, corresponding to ±x, ±y, ±z.

steps.prompt: Where does inversion map the +z domain?
steps.hint: Q is a polar vector.
choices: The −z domain, 180° from the original direction
To +z, because every parent-group operation preserves each domain
The +x domain
steps.explanation: Inversion reverses a polar vector, connecting positive and negative domains; it is outside the +z stabilizer.

steps.prompt: Does calculating six directions already give an actual  domain wall  width?
steps.hint: A uniform order parameter and spatial variations are separate questions.
choices: Yes; its width is 6 primitive cells
No; gradient, elastic, electrostatic, and other inputs are needed
Yes; the width is determined solely by 48/8
steps.explanation: The group index gives the number of equivalent directions, not the spatial structure or energy of a domain wall.

exercises.title: Recover the translational mode of two unequal-mass atoms
exercises.prompt: In a one-dimensional illustration, m1=1 and m2=4, and the mass-weighted real eigenvector is e=(1,2)/√5. Compare only relative displacements, with overall amplitude 1.

steps.prompt: How should masses be handled when recovering physical displacements from e?
steps.hint: dynamical matrix  is already normalized with square-root masses.
choices: uj=ej√mj
uj=ej/mj
uj=ej/√mj
steps.explanation: Multiplying by M^(−1/2) recovers the displacement direction in atomic coordinates.

steps.prompt: What is the resulting (u1,u2)?
steps.hint: Divide the second component, 2, by √4.

steps.prompt: What kind of motion is this?
steps.hint: Compare the directions and physical displacement lengths of the two atoms.
choices: Equal opposite optical motion
A rigid translation with equal displacements in the same direction
The second atom moves twice as far
steps.explanation: Equal physical displacements represent acoustic translation. The different lengths in e arise from mass weighting.

steps.prompt: Can doubling the overall animation amplitude establish the actual thermal amplitude?
steps.hint: The display scale includes no temperature, occupation number, or physical normalization.
choices: Yes; normalized e already gives absolute displacements
Yes; all modes have the same thermal amplitude
No; uniform enlargement changes only the display scale
steps.explanation: Relative mode shape and absolute mean-square displacement are distinct information; the latter requires additional dynamical and statistical inputs.

exercises.title: Find diffraction intensity using two phase arrows
exercises.prompt: Two scatterers in a cell lie at (0,0,0) and (1/2,0,0), both with constant weight 1. Use F=Σexp(2πih·x) and I=|F|².

steps.prompt: What is the second point's phase in the 100 reflection?
choices: π
steps.explanation: The second unit arrow rotates by π and points opposite to the first.

steps.prompt: What is (F,I) for 100?
steps.hint: Add complex amplitudes first, then take the squared modulus.
steps.explanation: F=1+(−1)=0, I=0; the two individual intensities cannot simply be added.

steps.prompt: What is (F,I) for 200?
steps.hint: The second point's phase becomes 2π.
steps.explanation: Two aligned unit arrows give F=2 and a squared modulus of 4.

steps.prompt: How does intensity change when all atoms are translated by the same δ?
steps.hint: Factor out the overall phase exp(2πih·δ).
choices: Changes arbitrarily with δ
It is unchanged
It must become zero
steps.explanation: Its modulus is 1, so translating the coordinate origin leaves the squared structure-factor modulus unchanged.

exercises.title: Identify the correct reasons for zero intensity in Si and GaAs
exercises.prompt: Calculate Si and GaAs using an F conventional cell with basis (0,0,0), (1/4,1/4,1/4). Initially take fSi=1; fGa and fAs can be set separately.

steps.prompt: Why does 100 vanish in both ideal structures?
steps.hint: Check the F-centering requirement first.
choices: Mixed parity of h,k,l makes the F-centering factor zero
Any odd h is forbidden
The two elements must have equal weights
steps.explanation: 100 has mixed parity, so LF=0 regardless of the basis weights.

steps.prompt: What additional mechanism makes Si 200 vanish?
steps.hint: 200 already satisfies the all-even condition.
choices: The F-centering factor is still zero
The two identical basis scatterers differ by phase π and cancel
200 cannot satisfy Bragg’s law at any wavelength
steps.explanation: LF=4, but 1+exp(iπ)=0: an additional cancellation from the diamond basis.

steps.prompt: For fGa=1 and fAs=2, what is GaAs 200 intensity?
steps.hint: F200=4(fGa−fAs)。
steps.explanation: F=−4, I=16; a negative amplitude is not a negative intensity.

steps.prompt: If fGa and fAs are both changed to 1, what does a zero 200 intensity mean?
steps.hint: Changing weights does not alter the  space group  occupations of the two elements.
choices: Cancellation in the present equal-weight model is not a universal forbidden reflection of this space group
Every GaAs 200 experiment must give exactly zero
The F lattice becomes an I lattice
steps.explanation: Equal weights make this particular amplitude vanish, unlike a space-group condition that applies to all compatible scattering weights.

exercises.title: Derive reflection sets from the operation itself
exercises.prompt: Compare 2₁(z): (x, y, z)→(−x,−y, z+1/2), with a c glide normal to x: (x, y, z)→(−x, y, z+1/2). Both preserve the scattering weights of connected sites.

steps.prompt: Which reflection vectors are preserved by the rotation part of 2₁(z)?
steps.hint: Require (−h,−k,l)=(h,k,l).
choices: Any hkl
All hk0
steps.explanation: It is strictly preserved only for h=k=0, so this operation alone gives a reflection-row condition.

steps.prompt: Along 00l, what allowed condition follows from the half-translation?
choices: l is even
l is odd
Any integer l is allowed and necessarily intense
steps.explanation: (−1)^l=1 requires even l; this operation forces odd-l reflections to vanish.

steps.prompt: To which set does the specified c-glide condition apply?
steps.hint: The mirror changes only the sign of h.
choices: All hkl
h00 with even h
0kl, even l
steps.explanation: Invariance requires h=0, while the translation phase requires even l, giving a condition within the reflection plane.

steps.prompt: Does satisfying this one condition guarantee a nonzero reflection?
steps.hint: Sum scattering contributions from the entire cell as well.
choices: Yes; satisfying the condition fixes the intensity
No; other symmetry conditions or the basis can still cause cancellation
Yes; intensity always equals atom count
steps.explanation: A reflection condition is necessary for avoiding a particular operation’s prohibition, but is not sufficient for a nonzero total amplitude.

exercises.title: Check a two-atom primitive-cell dataset before plotting
exercises.prompt: For Phonopy data of a specified natom=2, every q point contains a band list. Some files provide frequency only; others also provide eigenvector.

steps.prompt: How many modes should a complete q point have?
steps.hint: Each atom provides three Cartesian displacement coordinates.
steps.explanation: 3N=6; do not additionally subtract rotations at every q using isolated-molecule rules.

steps.prompt: How should eigenvector components [0.2,−0.1] be interpreted?
steps.hint: Phonopy writes the real part on the left and the imaginary part on the right.
choices: One Cartesian component 0.2−0.1i
The x displacements of two different atoms
Frequency and error bar
steps.explanation: Each atom's x, y, z components may be complex, each represented as [real part, imaginary part].

steps.prompt: With frequency data but no eigenvectors, which result remains supported by the data?
steps.hint: Do not infer atomic motion from frequency values alone.
choices: Reconstruct mode displacements exactly
Display the supplied frequencies and explicitly note that mode-animation data are missing
Automatically calculate Raman tensors
steps.explanation: Available frequencies can be displayed, but mode shapes and optical responses require independent information.

steps.prompt: Can an arbitrary qpoints list directly serve as a continuous dispersion and be integrated to obtain a DOS?
steps.hint: Check path connections and Brillouin-zone sampling weights.
choices: Yes; more than two q points suffice
Yes; just sort the coordinates
No; continuous paths and DOS each require appropriate sampling and weight information
steps.explanation: Connecting paths need not have been calculated between discrete points, and path sampling cannot replace a three-dimensional  Brillouin zone  integral.

exercises.title: Turn a negative frequency into a testable question
exercises.prompt: A phonon plot using the common negative-sign convention shows tiny negative values near Γ. Residual forces, supercell size, and electronic-sampling convergence have not yet been checked.

steps.prompt: What does this minus sign usually indicate?
steps.hint: The eigenvalue in the harmonic eigenproblem is ω².
choices: The atoms must vibrate in the negative direction
A display convention for negative eigenvalues of  dynamical matrix
The mode does not exist
steps.explanation: A negative eigenvalue gives an imaginary angular frequency, marked in plots by a negative real magnitude; it is not a negative stable oscillation period.

steps.prompt: What is the most appropriate conclusion now?
steps.hint: First distinguish a local harmonic indication from a reliable material conclusion.
choices: Check the reference state, units, and numerical convergence before judging whether negative curvature is reliable
The actual material cannot exist
The transition temperature has already been obtained
steps.explanation: Tiny negative values can reflect numerical error. Even reliable values retain temperature and anharmonicity limitations.

steps.prompt: What else is required to freeze displacements along a finite-q mode?
steps.hint: Finite-q phases must be compatible with periodic boundary conditions.
choices: Only the absolute frequency is needed
Move all atoms the same distance in any direction
Eigenvectors, masses, structure, correct phases and a compatible supercell
steps.explanation: Frequency alone cannot determine mode shape. At finite q, displacements must also be periodic in the chosen supercell.

steps.prompt: How can an energy curve verified along a known mode be used?
steps.hint: Compare small-amplitude energy changes with harmonic curvature before considering higher-order fits.
choices: One curve automatically gives the complete real phase diagram
Check directional curvature and fit a specified model, stating conditions and validity limits
Prove that every other mode is stable
steps.explanation: Frozen-mode validation provides evidence within a defined scope and can connect to Landau theory; it cannot replace stability analysis over all structures, temperatures, and wave vectors.

cases.name: BaTiO₃: from  polarity  distortion to directional domains
cases.summary: Connect an ideal cubic parent cell, an isolated Ti displacement, six equivalent directions, and a dimensionless double well into one teaching route.
cases.phase: An ideal Pm-3m parent structure; a small nonzero Ti displacement along +z gives a P4mm model, reducing the point group from m-3m to 4mm.
cases.question: Where are the two minima of F=−Q²+Q⁴? If polar directions are chosen along cubic axes, how many directional domains does the parent point group generate?
cases.answer: The one-dimensional slice has minima Q=±1/√2, both with free energy −1/4. The three-dimensional parent-group orbit of +z is ±x,±y,±z, giving six directional domains.
limitations: This is an idealized BaTiO₃-style teaching structure; it does not supply an actual temperature sequence, material Landau coefficients or a polarization value.
Moving only Ti does not represent a real soft-mode eigenvector. Coupled oxygen and barium motion, strain, and domain walls are not calculated.
A one-component free energy describes only a slice along one selected direction, not the complete three-dimensional anisotropic energy surface.
The built-in Phonopy example on the import page is synthetic data, not a BaTiO₃ calculation.

cases.name: Si: separate centering extinctions from diamond-basis extinctions
cases.summary: Diagnose extinctions successively using the 100, 200, and 220 reflections, then check six primitive-cell branches with your own phonon data.
cases.phase: Ideal  diamond structure  F  conventional cell  with identical atoms at basis positions (0,0,0) and (1/4,1/4,1/4); two atoms per  primitive cell .
cases.question: With the constant weight of each Si atom explicitly set to 1, why do both 100 and 200 vanish? What is the model intensity of 220?
cases.answer: 100 is extinguished by F centering; 200 satisfies the centering condition but is canceled by the identical-atom basis with a π phase difference; 220 gives F=8 and |F|²=64.
limitations: The hand exercise deliberately uses fSi=1. The calculator's default atomic-number weights differ; align inputs before comparing numbers.
This example does not generate actual Si phonon frequencies or experimental diffraction intensities.
For user-imported data, separately verify phase, primitive cell, masses, units, and calculation provenance.

cases.name: NaCl: sums and differences of two sublattices
cases.summary: Vary the two scattering weights separately to see how all-odd and all-even reflections probe sublattice differences and sums.
cases.phase: An F-centered conventional cell of ideal rock salt; the Cl basis offset relative to Na is (1/2,1/2,1/2), with two atoms per primitive cell.
cases.question: With constant model weights fNa=1 and fCl=2, find the 111 and 200 structure factors and model intensities.
cases.answer: F111=4(1−2)=−4, I111=16; F200=4(1+2)=12, I200=144. Both pass F-centering conditions; their difference comes from basis phases.
limitations: Constant integer weights are used only for derivation; they are not NaCl X-ray atomic form factors or neutron scattering lengths.
The two elements have different masses, so Phonopy eigenvectors must be converted to relative displacements using their respective masses.
The existing IR-activity lesson connects to the new importer, but imported frequencies alone do not calculate effective charges.

cases.name: GaAs: how does chemical occupancy remove basis cancellation?
cases.summary: Keep the same offset geometry as Si and vary only the two scatterer weights to distinguish chemical contrast from universal reflection conditions.
cases.phase: Ideal zinc-blende F conventional cell, with Ga and As at basis positions (0,0,0) and (1/4,1/4,1/4); two atoms per primitive cell.
cases.question: For 200, how do fGa=1 and fAs=2 differ from the model with both weights 1? Which conclusion generalizes to a universal F-lattice condition?
cases.answer: For different weights, F200=−4 and I=16; equal weights cancel exactly. F centering forbids 100 in both cases. The equal-weight zero at 200 is not a universal condition of the zinc-blende space group.
limitations: The model changes specified scattering weights; equal weights do not turn chemically distinct Ga and As into the same atomic species.
Actual intensities also depend on scattering conditions. Default atomic-number weights are not a complete angle-dependent scattering model.
Importing data and demonstrating eigenvectors do not automatically provide GaAs LO–TO splitting, effective charges or Raman tensors.
